title: Law school admissions expert sees 'dangerous one-two punch' as Gen Z seeks shelter from the AI hiring storm in 6-figure debt and law-degree lifeboat
author: Jake Angelo

kp.k: Law school applications surge amid entry-level hiring weakness
kp.d: The article reports applicants rising more than 40% over the past two years, citing ABA data compiled by LSAC. Mike Spivey attributes the overwhelming majority of the increase to hiring difficulties rather than students’ concerns about the rule of law under the Trump administration; his 90% attribution is presented as his assessment, not a measured causal finding.
qs: the number of applicants up more than 40% over the past two years, according to American Bar Association (ABA) data compiled by the Law School Admission Council (LSAC).
“While we’re not in an economic recession, we’re in a hiring recession,” Spivey said. “And that’s 90% of it.”

kp.k: Recent graduate employment remains strong despite prospective risks
kp.d: The article contrasts fears about legal careers with reported employment outcomes: over 80% of graduates in 2023 and 2024 held jobs requiring their legal credentials within a year, according to the ABA, while NALP claimed a record overall graduate employment rate exceeding 93% in 2024. These are distinct employment measures, and the article does not present them as evidence of AI-driven displacement.
qs: over 80% of graduates in 2023 and 2024 working in jobs that require their legal credentials within a year, according to the ABA.
In 2024 the National Association for Law Placement claimed the highest employment rate ever for law school grads, at more than 93%.

kp.k: Growing graduate supply could coincide with reduced hiring
kp.d: Spivey predicts that oversaturation will let law firms become more selective and slow hiring or salary increases. He warns that rising law school participation combined with potentially weaker recruitment could leave current entrants exposed. This is a prospective supply-and-demand argument, not evidence that AI has already reduced hiring.
qs: “When you get an oversaturation of law school students, law firms can be pickier. They tend to then slow down the hiring or slow down the salary increases.”
“You have more people going to law school and the possibility of law firms not hiring as much,” Spivey said. “That’s a dangerous one-two punch.”

kp.k: Recession could make AI substitution for juniors persistent
kp.d: Jen Leonard predicts that an economic downturn could eliminate junior associate roles and prompt firms and clients to substitute AI for some labor to maintain competitiveness. She explicitly expresses uncertainty about whether entry-level recruitment would recover with the economy, distinguishing this possible structural change from ordinary cyclical job losses.
qs: “The firms and the clients will figure out how to use AI to some degree [to] replace that labor,” Leonard told
“When the economy rebounds, I don’t know that you would see a rebound in entry-level hiring the way you normally would.”

kp.k: Historical downturns underpin the law-school shelter argument
kp.d: The article compares the current application surge with increases in 2008 and 2020 and cites LSAC historical data showing LSAT participation rising over 15% after the 2008 financial crisis. It qualifies the analogy by noting that the economy is not currently shrinking, while citing the Federal Reserve Bank of New York for recent graduates’ unemployment exceeding that of all workers for the first time in the available data.
qs: LSAC historical data shows that in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis the number of people taking the LSAT rose over 15%.

the unemployment rate for recent college graduates has surpassed the unemployment rate for all workers for the first time since data became available, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

kp.k: Firms integrate AI assistants to improve legal workflows
kp.d: The article reports AI adoption for routine work and workflow optimization, identifying A&O Shearman and Macfarlanes as integrating Harvey AI into core operations and DLA Piper and Fisher Phillips as adopting Thomson Reuters’s CoCounsel. These examples establish reported adoption, without quantified productivity results or demonstrated employment effects.
qs: Some law firms have adopted AI to take on grunt work and to optimize workflows.
Firms such as A&O Shearman and Macfarlanes have integrated Harvey AI, an AI legal assistant, into their core operations.
Other firms are seizing upon Thomson Reuters’s CoCounsel—DLA Piper and Fisher Phillips, among them.

kp.k: Eudia presents AI-native delivery as challenging hourly billing
kp.d: The article reports Eudia’s ambition to eliminate the billable hour and its self-description as an AI-native law firm. This is a provider’s stated positioning and intended pricing disruption, not evidence that hourly billing has been displaced.
qs: And one AI startup, the Palo Alto–based Eudia, has vowed to kill the billable hour, describing itself as “the first AI-native law firm.”

kp.k: Risk aversion delays hiring effects despite deepening adoption
kp.d: Spivey says AI adoption has not yet affected hiring processes because law firms are cautious. He describes adverse publicity about legal AI failures as prompting retreat, while predicting progressively deeper adoption as firms return to experimentation. The account qualifies the article’s displacement concerns: they remain prospective rather than observed hiring effects in his assessment.
qs: Yet Spivey said that AI adoption hasn’t yet had an impact on hiring processes, mainly owing to the overly cautious nature of law firms.

“They are trained to be risk averse, so they put their little pinky toe in the pool,” Spivey said. “Every time there’s a horrible media story about AI failing in the legal profession, they take it out of the pool.”
“Every time they put [their toe] back in, they put it in deeper.”

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The article reports current AI use for productivity, while contrasting limited present hiring effects with predictions of future entry-level substitution.
pts.d: Jake Angelo reports that firms are adopting AI for routine work and workflow optimization, identifying Harvey AI use at A&O Shearman and Macfarlanes and CoCounsel use at DLA Piper and Fisher Phillips. He also reports Eudia's stated ambition to eliminate the billable hour, not an achieved pricing transformation. Mike Spivey says AI adoption has not yet affected hiring processes because law firms are cautious, but predicts progressively deeper adoption. Jen Leonard predicts that a downturn could eliminate junior associate roles and that AI substitution by firms and clients could prevent the customary recovery in entry-level hiring. Separately, Spivey's warning about growing law-school cohorts and slower hiring concerns labour supply and hiring conditions; it is not itself evidence of AI displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Named adoption examples support the account of current use; hiring and substitution claims rest on interviewees' assessments rather than measured AI employment effects.
pts.d: Angelo supplies examples of named firms using Harvey AI and CoCounsel, but no quantified productivity results. Leonard's forecast is an expert assessment from the founder of Creative Lawyers, not a documented finding about job losses. Spivey's account of cautious adoption and no current hiring impact is attributed to him as CEO of a law-school admissions consultancy; the article supplies no hiring study isolating AI's effects. Eudia's billable-hour claim is a reported company ambition. The article provides contextual applicant and employment statistics: applicants increased more than 40% over two years, over 80% of 2023 and 2024 graduates obtained jobs requiring legal credentials within a year, and NALP reported employment above 93% in 2024. Those statistics describe admissions and graduate employment, not causal effects of AI.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Present adoption is distinguished from undated future changes, with Leonard's displacement scenario conditional on a downturn and subsequent recovery.
pts.d: As of the article's January 26, 2026 publication, Angelo reports existing AI deployments, and Spivey says hiring has not yet been affected by AI. Leonard's scenario concerns a future economic downturn followed by recovery: firms would use AI to remain competitive, potentially reducing the return of junior jobs. Her wording expresses uncertainty about that recovery rather than a definite forecast of permanent elimination of all entry-level roles. Spivey predicts deeper adoption over time without a date, describing setbacks when negative coverage of AI failures reinforces firms' risk aversion. No deadline is given for Eudia's billable-hour ambition.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Prospective graduates and junior associates face the predicted employment risks; firms and clients are described as potential adopters substituting AI for junior labour.
pts.d: Leonard's displacement prediction specifically concerns junior associates and entry-level hiring, rather than demonstrated profession-wide job losses. The article connects this risk to Gen Z graduates entering law school amid weak hiring and increasing applicant numbers. Law firms are adopting tools for routine tasks and workflows, while both firms and clients are identified by Leonard as actors that may replace some labour with AI. Eudia's stated ambition concerns the hourly billing model; the article does not quantify consequences for fees, firm revenues, or client savings.
